evals.prompt: I just got assigned to this repo and I need to own it fast. Can you coach me on this codebase?
evals.expected_output: The coach silently inspects the repo using file tools, then delivers a compact orient (≤10 bullets), then asks exactly ONE architecture-level question to kick off the Socratic loop. It does NOT ask compound questions. It does NOT lecture or summarize the full codebase. It distinguishes inferences from facts.
assertions: The response includes evidence that the coach read repo files before producing output (reads package.json, directory structure, or similar)
The orient section has 10 or fewer bullet points
The response ends with exactly one question (not multiple questions)
The opening question targets architecture or entrypoints (not extension points or blast radius — those come later)
The response does NOT provide the answer to its own question immediately after asking it

evals.prompt: I built this project myself 6 months ago, barely remember how it works. Quiz me hard on the architecture.
evals.expected_output: The coach inspects the repo, delivers a brief orient, then asks a harder or more targeted question befitting someone who was the author (e.g., asking about design decisions, trade-offs, or why something is structured a certain way). It adapts to the signal that this is not a total beginner.
assertions: The response includes evidence that the coach read repo files before producing output
The first question goes beyond surface-level naming (it asks about responsibilities, flows, or design decisions rather than just 'what is in this directory')
The response ends with exactly one question
The question is phrased as active recall (e.g. 'Where does X live?' or 'What would happen if...') not a yes/no question

evals.prompt: Teach me this codebase. I want to understand it well enough to make changes without breaking things.
evals.expected_output: The coach inspects the repo, orients the user, asks one architecture question. The brief orient includes at least one non-obvious observation (a sharp edge, an implicit invariant, a surprising coupling, or an unusual pattern) rather than just listing directories.
assertions: The response includes evidence that the coach read repo files before producing output
The orient includes at least one non-obvious observation (a risk, sharp edge, implicit invariant, or notable pattern — not just naming directories and files)
The response ends with exactly one question
The question requires genuine recall or reasoning, not a lookup (it cannot be answered by just reading the file name)
